ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Viral receptors are host cell surface proteins that viruses bind to for entry. Their identity determines which tissues a virus infects, influences disease severity, and guides prevention and treatment strategies.

sections.p: Viruses cannot replicate without entering a host cell. They achieve this by attaching to specific proteins, glycolipids, or sugars on the cell surface—called viral receptors. The match between viral surface proteins (spikes) and host receptors dictates tropism and clinical manifestations.
b: Receptor–virus binding is the first step of infection
Receptor distribution explains organ‑specific disease patterns
Mutations in viral spikes can expand or shift receptor use, affecting pandemic potential

sections.p: Each virus encodes one or more surface proteins (e.g., hemagglutinin, spike, gp120) that recognize a host receptor. Structural studies show a lock‑and‑key interaction that can be blocked by antibodies or drugs.
b: Spike proteins are immunogenic targets for vaccines
Receptor binding affinity correlates with transmissibility

sections.p: After binding its receptor, the virus is internalized by endocytosis or membrane fusion, releases its genome, replicates, assembles new virions, and exits to infect new cells. The receptor determines the portal of entry (respiratory, gastrointestinal, neuronal).
b: Respiratory viruses often use sialic acid (influenza) or ACE2 (SARS‑CoV‑2)
Enteric viruses may bind CD55 (coxsackie) or histo‑blood group antigens

sections.p: Clinical disease reflects the cells that express the viral receptor. For example, ACE2 expression in lung alveolar type II cells leads to COVID‑19 pneumonia, while CD4 on T‑cells leads to HIV immunodeficiency.
Identify the virus and, when relevant, the receptor it uses. This guides infection control and therapeutic choices.
b: Molecular detection of viral genome (PCR) confirms infection
Serology shows exposure but not receptor use

t.b: Which virus is present? Positive result confirms infection and allows inference of receptor based on known virus‑receptor pairs.
Does the virus use a specific receptor? Positive entry in receptor‑expressing cells confirms receptor usage; unavailable in low‑resource labs → rely on epidemiology and known virus patterns.

sections.p: Therapy targets the virus and, when possible, blocks receptor interaction. Prevention focuses on vaccines that generate antibodies to the viral spike.
b: Monoclonal antibodies that block spike‑receptor binding (e.g., anti‑spike for SARS‑CoV‑2)
Entry inhibitors (e.g., maraviroc blocks CCR5 for HIV)
Vaccines induce neutralising antibodies to the receptor‑binding domain

sections.p: Key points to remember for exams:
b: High‑affinity receptor binding often predicts higher transmissibility
Therapies that block receptor binding are virus‑specific

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid respiratory failure in influenza or COVID‑19
Severe immunosuppression with opportunistic infections in HIV

faq.q: Why do some viruses cause severe disease while others are mild?
faq.a: Severity depends on receptor distribution, binding affinity, and the host immune response; widespread receptors can lead to systemic illness.

faq.q: Can a virus use more than one receptor?
faq.a: Yes; some viruses (e.g., adenovirus) bind multiple receptors, broadening tissue tropism and clinical presentations.

faq.q: How does receptor knowledge help vaccine design?
faq.a: Vaccines target the viral protein that contacts the receptor, generating antibodies that block entry.

exam: Explain how the distribution of ACE2 explains the primary clinical features of COVID‑19.
Describe two ways a mutation in a viral spike protein can alter pandemic potential.
List three therapeutic strategies that target viral receptor interactions and state why each is chosen.
